Also, the cold water and warm water pumps as well as the refrigerant pumps and turbine/generator will likely require maintenance and replacements during the life of the facility, making accessibility for their removal important. Dedicating the vertical space above a hatch cover on the top of the hull column to be a maintenance zone (for raising and lowering equipment into the hull column using the platform crane) limits the usability of the already limited topsides space, so other options should also be explored. In addition, lighting and ventilating the hull column sufficiently for daily access for operator rounds of equipment surveillance adds to the capital costs (unless there is other oil and gas equipment in the hull column that already required such amenities). Utilization of cameras and vapor space monitors for refrigerant leaks could potentially reduce the frequency of physical visits inside the hull column. 4.2.2 Medium (1 MW) and Maximum (3.9 MW) Add-On As alluded to in the previous section, given the current state of the equipment available to design an OTEC plant and the marine resources of the GOA, in order to reach net power capacity exceeding an annual average of 100 kW on a single unit (or 400 kW in a scenario where OTEC equipment is in four hull columns of a typical semi-submersible), the OTEC plant must be outside of the platform’s hull columns. Therefore, the next two designs are considered “Add-On” whereby a self-buoyant enclosure that houses all or parts of the equipment is attached to the exterior frame of the platform hull. Like with the hull- integrated scenario above, the add-on concepts also consider addition to a newly deployed facility, and not a retrofit to an existing facility, although a retrofit to accommodate an add- on would be possible and far less cost-prohibitive than a hull integrated OTEC. The 1 MW and 3.9 MW designs use similar equipment except the different-sized cold-water intake pipe diameters.
